title: Deployed entanglement-based BBM92 quantum key distribution using frequency-converted photons emitted by a quantum dot
authors: Michal Vyvlecka, Raphael Joos, Benjamin Breiholz, Emma Marmasse, Ilenia Neureuther, Timo Schnieber, Anna Frederike Köhler, Tim Strobel, Andreas Berg, Sebastian Kiesel, Tobias Bauer, Marlon Schäfer, Nand Lal Sharma, Caspar Hopfmann, Simone Luca Portalupi, Christoph Becher, Peter Michler
abstract: Establishing secure communication is an important requirement in existing and future networks. Although current solutions rely on classical approaches, quantum mechanics offers the possibility of moving from computational to information-theoretic security. Quantum key distribution (QKD) has been extensively studied as a means of achieving such security. Recently, epitaxial quantum dots started to be studied and employed in quantum cryptography, because of their rapid development that made them one of the brightest sources of quantum light to date. In particular, they are known to be excellent sources of polarization-entangled photon pairs, especially droplet-etched dots operating at $\sim$780 nm. Here, we employ such a quantum dot to generate entangled photon pairs under 1 GHz excitation rate. Using quantum frequency conversion, we interface the emitted photons with the telecommunication wavelength range while preserving their polarization entanglement. This enables quantum key distribution over a 1.59 km field-deployed fibre link across the University of Stuttgart - campus Vaihingen, using the BBM92 protocol: we achieve a secure key rate of 206 Hz over 19 h of stable operation, resulting in a total secure key length of 14.2 Mbit. This key enables the safe encryption and decryption of a colour image with further implementation of error correction and privacy amplification. These results demonstrate important steps towards hybrid quantum networks by combining high-quality entangled-photon sources operated at high excitation rates, efficient frequency conversion module, and picosecond-level time synchronization in a realistic deployed network.
summary: This paper reports on a successful field deployment of an entanglement-based Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) system using quantum dots as the entangled photon source. By employing quantum frequency conversion, the system transmits quantum signals over a 1.59 km fiber link, achieving a stable secure key rate of 206 Hz. The results mark a significant step toward realizing hybrid, long-distance quantum networks.
main_problem: The paper addresses the critical need for information-theoretic security in communication networks by demonstrating Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) over a deployed fiber link.
main_result: The authors successfully achieved a secure key rate of 206 Hz over a 1.59 km deployed fiber link, generating a total secure key length of 14.2 Mbit.
method: They implemented the entanglement-based BBM92 protocol, utilizing quantum dots as entangled photon sources and quantum frequency conversion to bridge the emission wavelength to the telecom band.
model_or_system: The system uses epitaxial quantum dots excited via two-photon excitation to generate polarization-entangled photon pairs at $\sim 780 	ext{ nm}$. These photons are then frequency-converted to the telecom C-band ($\sim 1550 	ext{ nm}$) for transmission over a real-world fiber link.
key_observables: Secure key rate (206 Hz), total secure key length (14.2 Mbit), and fidelity of the entangled state (91.4%).
important_parameters: Fiber link distance of 1.59 km; QD fine-structure splitting ($\delta=2.1(3) \mu	ext{eV}$); repetition rate of 1 GHz.
main_assumptions: The successful integration relies on high-quality entangled sources, efficient quantum frequency conversion, and picosecond-level time synchronization in a deployed network.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the experimental setup map and the source configuration involving QD emission and QFC. Figure 2 likely shows the dependence of key rates and QBER on coincidence window timing. Figure 3 compares the encrypted and decrypted color images.
paper_structure: The paper follows a structure detailing the problem (secure communication), the physical platform (QD source + QFC), the protocol implementation (BBM92), the experimental results (key rate, key length), and concluding with the demonstration of practical network integration.
why_interesting: This work is highly relevant as it demonstrates the practical engineering required to move quantum communication from lab bench demonstrations to real-world, deployed infrastructure, which is a major goal in quantum networking.

Key experimental figures: Key rate, secure key rate, and QBER. a) Observed raw key rate (RKR) (left scale) and QBER (right scale) as a function of the coincidence window used for the detection of the two photons. For a coincidence window of 275 ps, the secure key rate (SKR) reaches its maximum of 204 Hz, with an RKR of 502 Hz, while maintaining a QBER of 4.71 %, well below the the- oretical security threshold of 11 % for the present protocol. b) Raw key rate (left scale) and QBER (right scale) as a function of time during the 19 h-long measurement. The plotted values are hourly av- erages. The QBER remains well below the 11 % security threshold (gray dashed line) for this protocol.

(top) The original 24-bit colour image with a resolution of 943×620 pixels (shown under the gray box indicating the quantum-channel characteristics, including the measurement time and QBER) is encrypted with the raw key (left side, orange) or with the secure key (right side, green). Decryption using the raw key (bottom left) or the secure key (bottom right), after error correction and privacy amplification with an effective retention ratio of PAe f f =40.48 %. For both decrypted images, a zoom of the same respective areas highlights the removal of corrupted pixels after decryption with the secure key.
